planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained sandy soil in part shade; Coastal Azalea is a low, suckering native deciduous azalea of the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, naturally forming spreading colonies in sandy pine woods rather than a single upright shrub.

directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, humus-rich, acidic, sandy soil in part shade, mimicking the open pine woodland and coastal plain scrub where it grows wild. Coastal Azalea is one of the lowest-growing of the native deciduous azaleas, spreading by root suckers into loose colonies rather than staying as a single tidy shrub, which makes it useful as a woodland-edge groundcover or naturalized drift rather than a formal specimen. Its fragrant white to pale pink flowers, sometimes with a yellow blotch, open in mid-spring before or with the emerging foliage and carry a sweet, clove-like scent that carries well on the breeze. Unlike many native azaleas that prefer consistently moist streambank soil, Coastal Azalea tolerates drier, sandier conditions once established, reflecting its native habitat on the coastal plain, though it still benefits from a thick mulch layer and supplemental water during dry spells. Prune only to remove dead wood, since it needs little shaping to look at home in a naturalistic planting.

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; Confetti Lantana is a low, spreading trailing selection with multicolor pink-orange-yellow flower clusters, useful in hanging baskets, containers, and as a groundcover in full sun.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil, and avoid overwatering or heavy fertilization, since lean, dry conditions produce the most flowers and best drought tolerance. Confetti is a low, spreading, trailing lantana cultivar whose flower clusters open yellow and shift through orange to rosy pink as they age, so each cluster shows several colors at once for a lively, multicolored effect across the whole plant. Its cascading habit makes it a strong choice for hanging baskets, window boxes, and spilling over the edge of raised beds or retaining walls, in addition to its use as a fast, heat-tolerant flowering groundcover in a sunny bed. Like other lantanas it draws in butterflies steadily from spring to frost without needing deadheading, and it shrugs off the worst of Gulf Coast summer heat and drought better than almost any other bedding plant. In the warmest parts of its range it can persist as a woody perennial, dying back in a light freeze and resprouting from the base in spring.

common_name: Plum Gorgeous Loropetalum (Compact Deep Plum-Purple Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Plum Gorgeous is a compact, mounding loropetalum selection grown for deep plum-purple foliage that holds its color well through the growing season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with at least a few hours of direct sun each day to bring out the deepest foliage color, since plants grown in heavy shade fade toward green. Plum Gorgeous is a compact, mounding loropetalum selected for rich, deep plum-purple foliage that holds its color through summer heat better than many older loropetalum cultivars, paired with bright pink fringe flowers that appear in a heavy spring flush and continue sporadically into summer and fall. Its manageable, rounded size fits foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders without the frequent shearing larger loropetalums need to stay in bounds, and the dark foliage makes an effective color contrast against golden or chartreuse companion plants. Loropetalums as a group are among the most heat- and humidity-tolerant flowering shrubs for the Gulf South and are largely trouble-free once established in well-drained soil; avoid waterlogged sites, which invite root rot.

common_name: Prince Tut Papyrus (Medium Dwarf Egyptian Papyrus)

planting.note: Grow in a submerged aquatic pot of heavy garden soil so the crown and lower stems sit an inch or two underwater at the pond's edge, or in consistently saturated soil; Prince Tut is a medium-sized dwarf papyrus, taller than Baby Tut but more compact than King Tut, well suited to a mid-sized container water garden.

directions: Set potted divisions into a submerged aquatic container of heavy garden soil so the crown and lower stems sit an inch or two underwater along the pond's edge, or grow it in a large container of constantly saturated soil kept in a saucer of water. Prince Tut is a mid-sized dwarf selection of Egyptian papyrus, taller and fuller than the very compact Baby Tut but noticeably more manageable than full-sized King Tut, forming a dense clump of slender, leafless stems topped with fine, mop-like tufts of thread-like bracts that sway in the breeze. It brings strong vertical, textural interest to a water garden or bog planting and works equally well in a large mixed container as a dramatic thriller element, provided its roots stay constantly wet. Outside its hardy range it is grown as a warm-season annual or brought indoors and kept in a water-filled saucer over winter as a houseplant.

common_name: Baby Tut Papyrus (Compact Miniature Egyptian Papyrus)

planting.note: Grow in a submerged aquatic pot of heavy garden soil so the crown sits at or just below the water's surface, or in a small container kept constantly saturated; Baby Tut is the most compact of the dwarf papyrus selections, well suited to small water features and tabletop containers.

directions: Set potted divisions into a submerged aquatic container of heavy garden soil with the crown at or just below the waterline, or grow it in a small pot kept constantly saturated in a saucer of water. Baby Tut is the smallest of the dwarf Egyptian papyrus selections, forming a tidy clump of slender stems only a foot or so tall topped with miniature mop-like tufts, making it practical for a small tabletop water garden, the shallow margin of a compact pond, or a mixed container where full-sized papyrus would overwhelm the planting. Its diminutive scale doesn't reduce its need for constant moisture, since papyrus in any size still wants its roots sitting in water or fully saturated soil at all times to thrive. Outside its hardy range, grow it as a warm-season annual or bring the pot indoors for winter, keeping it in a water-filled saucer on a bright windowsill.
